newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER SHOWCASE-ROBERTO CARLOS WORKS HARD AT FREE-KICKS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-ROBERTO CARLOS WORKS HARD AT FREE-KICKS.

text.p: Roberto Carlos, Brazil's hero after his remarkable swerving free-kick against France, has no hesitation in agreeing it was one of the 10 best goals ever.

"Yes, I think so, and I scored another with my instep against Celta (in a Spanish league match)," the Real Madrid left back said. The shot against Celta rose over the wall then dipped sharply into the net.

Roberto Carlos is happy because the goal he scored in Brazil's 1-1 draw with France in the opening match of the Tournoi de France on Tuesday strengthens his claim on a place in his country's 1998 World Cup side.

"There are so many great players in the national team. I feel important too, doing important things for the team," he said in an interview ahead of Brazil's meeting with Italy, a repeat of the 1994 final, on Sunday.

In Tuesday's match, Roberto Carlos gave Brazil the lead in the 21st minute when he scored from 35 metres, putting such a swerve on the ball with the outside of his left foot that it bent to the right round France's four-man wall and curled into the net off the post.
It was his second goal for Brazil in 30 internationals, the first coming against Japan in a 3-0 victory in the Umbro Cup in England in 1995.
Roberto Carlos says he works at his free-kicks every day and the only secret is concentration.
"I always practise, every day. I prefer to kick with the outside of my foot. There's no secret, it's much more (a question of) concentration," he said.
He said any one of several players in the team could take free-kicks -- central defender Celio Silva took Brazil's other long-range one.
"When I saw where we had the free-kick I felt confident. I said 'I'm okay to shoot', so (captain) Dunga said that's good."
France's goalkeeper Fabien Barthez said afterwards he was to blame for the goal, for not lining up his wall properly.
But Roberto Carlos said: "He didn't make a mistake. The wall was well placed. The ball went a long way off (the line of) the goal, then came back fast."
Dunga said: "I knew that if he got his shot on target the ball would go in. I simply advised him to put a bit of swerve on it."
French playmaker Zinedine Zidane said: "When you have a guy like that in your team, capable of shooting from any position and giving the ball any direction he wants, it's a hell of a plus."
Roberto Carlos, now 24, began his career as a forward at Uniao Sao Joao at 16 and represented Brazil for the first time at 18 in the 1992 Olympic qualifying tournament.
Endowed with a very powerful shot, he moved to Palmeiras. "I scored another great goal during play against Sa Paulo, from the left, that went in the top far corner."

As a full-back he has won more plaudits for his attacking play than his defending yet he was unhappy for four months at Inter Milan where the club's English coach Roy Hodgson moved him up into midfield.

Roberto Carlos, overlooked for the 1994 World Cup finals where Branco and Leonardo were preferred, likes his position. "I like to go up along the touchline but I also like defending. I'm learning to defend more," he said.
Paris St Germain could have had him for about $3 million in 1995. Instead he went to Inter for some $7 million.
After one season he moved on to Real, joining another of the Spanish club's Italian signings, coach Fabio Capello. Both are on the point of celebrating the league title.
